images.title: Count the unit squares
images.purpose: Show that area is the count of unit squares, rows times columns, so the 7 cm by 4 cm rectangle beats the 8 cm by 3 cm one.
images.composition: Two rectangles side by side on one baseline, drawn with the same size unit squares, the area written under each.
images.exact_structure: Plain white background, the main figure large and centred with generous empty margins on all sides, thin dark outlines (#2B2B2B), flat fills, nothing else in the frame. Left: a rectangle 7 squares wide and 4 squares tall, filled with exactly 28 equal unit squares (7 columns, 4 rows), light #0072B2 fill with thin grid lines. Right: a rectangle 8 squares wide and 3 squares tall, filled with exactly 24 equal unit squares (8 columns, 3 rows), light #E69F00 fill. All unit squares in both rectangles are the same size; both rectangles sit on the same baseline with a wide gap between them. Label '7 cm' centred under the left rectangle's bottom edge and '4 cm' beside its left edge; '8 cm' under the right rectangle's bottom edge and '3 cm' beside its left edge. Below each rectangle its area in bold: '28 cm²' under the left, '24 cm²' under the right; the '28 cm²' has a thin #CC79A7 outline box to mark the larger area.
rejection: any count of objects, cells, ticks or rows that differs from the numbers stated in the spec
any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
a hyphen used in place of a minus sign on any labelled number
images.takeaway: Area counts unit squares: 7 × 4 = 28 is more than 8 × 3 = 24.
images.description: Show that area is the count of unit squares, rows times columns, so the 7 cm by 4 cm rectangle beats the 8 cm by 3 cm one.
images.context: Concept T2.C1; one image showing only the main idea.

image_decisions.why: The concept's whole idea is the count of unit squares in its two rectangles; seeing the grids makes length times width visible.
